title: Das kluge Grethel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 77. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fiengen, thun/thue/that, Hausthüre, Grethel, ward).
about: KHM 77, a kitchen farce in which a servant’s wits are turned on her own household. Grethel is set to roast two chickens for her master’s guest; she tastes, drinks, eats both, and then — with the carving knife being whetted out in the passage — tells the arriving guest that her master means to cut off his ears, and sends the two men chasing each other out of the story. Note that the tale keeps slipping from sie to the neuter es for Grethel (das Mädel is grammatically neuter), so the literal line often says “it” where English must say “she”; spelling follows the 1857 edition, with Grethel, thun/that, gahr and rothen.

sentences.t: Es war eine Köchin, die hieß Grethel, die trug Schuhe mit rothen Absätzen, und wenn sie damit ausgieng, so drehte sie sich hin und her, war ganz fröhlich, und dachte „du bist doch ein schönes Mädel.“
sentences.l: There was a cook, she was called Grethel, she wore shoes with red heels, and when she went out in them, so she turned herself this way and that, was quite merry, and thought “you are indeed a fine girl.”
sentences.i: There was once a cook named Grethel, who wore shoes with red heels; and when she went out in them, she turned herself this way and that, thoroughly pleased, and thought: “You are a handsome girl, and no mistake.”
sentences.n: Grethel keeps the 1857 spelling (modern Gretel). Red heels were showy finery, well above a kitchen servant’s station. She talks to herself as du — she will do it all through the tale, and she is the only company she needs.

sentences.t: Und wenn sie nach Haus kam, so trank sie aus Fröhlichkeit einen Schluck Wein, und weil der Wein auch Lust zum Essen macht, so versuchte sie das beste, was sie kochte, so lang, bis sie satt war, und sprach „die Köchin muß wissen wies Essen schmeckt.“
sentences.l: And when she came home, so she drank out of merriment a swallow of wine, and because the wine also makes desire for eating, so she tasted the best of what she cooked, so long until she was full, and said “the cook must know how the food tastes.”
sentences.i: And when she came home she would drink a mouthful of wine out of sheer merriment; and because wine also makes one hungry, she would taste the best of whatever she was cooking, and keep at it until she was full, and say: “The cook must know how the food tastes.”
sentences.n: versuchen here is not “to try” in the modern sense but the older “to taste, to sample” — the excuse the whole tale rests on. wies = wie es.

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß der Herr einmal zu ihr sagte „Grethel, heut Abend kommt ein Gast, richte mir zwei Hühner fein wohl zu.“
sentences.l: It bore itself to pass that the master once said to her “Grethel, this evening a guest is coming, prepare me two chickens right well.”
sentences.i: It came to pass that her master said to her one day: “Grethel, a guest is coming this evening; get me two chickens ready, and do them nicely.”

sentences.t: „Wills schon machen, Herr,“ antwortete Grethel.
sentences.l: “Will already do it, sir,” answered Grethel.
sentences.i: “I’ll see to it, sir,” answered Grethel.
sentences.n: Wills = will es, with the subject ich simply dropped, as in casual speech: “[I] will [do] it.” schon here reassures — never fear, it will be done.

sentences.t: Nun stachs die Hühner ab, brühte sie, rupfte sie, steckte sie an den Spieß, und brachte sie, wies gegen Abend gieng, zum Feuer, damit sie braten sollten.
sentences.l: Now it stuck the chickens dead, scalded them, plucked them, stuck them on the spit, and brought them, as it went toward evening, to the fire, so that they should roast.
sentences.i: Now she killed the chickens, scalded them, plucked them, set them on the spit and, as it drew on toward evening, brought them to the fire to roast.
sentences.n: stachs = stach es, and that es is Grethel. From here the tale keeps slipping from sie to the neuter es (das Mädel is grammatically neuter), so the “it” of the literal line is always her. abstechen is to kill by sticking, as a bird or a pig is slaughtered. wies = wie es.

sentences.t: Die Hühner fiengen an braun und gahr zu werden, aber der Gast war noch nicht gekommen.
sentences.l: The chickens began to become brown and done, but the guest had not yet come.
sentences.i: The chickens were beginning to turn brown and to be done, but the guest had not yet come.

sentences.t: Da rief Grethel dem Herrn, „kommt der Gast nicht, so muß ich die Hühner vom Feuer thun, ist aber Jammer und Schade wenn sie nicht bald gegessen werden, wo sie am besten im Saft sind.“
sentences.l: Then called Grethel to the master, “comes the guest not, so must I take the chickens from the fire, but it is misery and pity if they are not soon eaten, when they are best in the juice.”
sentences.i: Then Grethel called to her master: “If the guest does not come, I must take the chickens off the fire; but it is a crying shame if they are not eaten soon, while they are at their juiciest.”
sentences.n: “kommt der Gast nicht, so…” is a condition with no wenn — the verb simply stands first. “Jammer und Schade” is a fixed pair, a crying shame; “im Saft sein” is to be at one’s juiciest.

sentences.t: Sprach der Herr „so will ich nur selbst laufen und den Gast holen.“
sentences.l: Spoke the master “so will I just run myself and fetch the guest.”
sentences.i: Said the master: “Then I shall just go myself and fetch the guest.”

sentences.t: Als der Herr den Rücken gekehrt hatte, legte Grethel den Spieß mit den Hühnern beiseite und dachte „so lange da beim Feuer stehen, macht schwitzen und durstig, wer weiß wann die kommen! derweil spring ich in den Keller und thue einen Schluck.“
sentences.l: When the master had turned his back, laid Grethel the spit with the chickens aside and thought “to stand so long there by the fire makes one sweat and thirsty, who knows when they will come! meanwhile I spring into the cellar and take a swallow.”
sentences.i: When the master had turned his back, Grethel laid the spit with the chickens aside and thought: “Standing so long there by the fire makes one sweat and grow thirsty — who knows when they will come! In the meantime I shall slip down to the cellar and take a swallow.”

sentences.t: Lief hinab, setzte einen Krug an, sprach „Gott gesegnes dir, Grethel,“ und that einen guten Zug.
sentences.l: Ran down, set a jug to her lips, spoke “God bless it to you, Grethel,” and took a good draught.
sentences.i: Down she ran, put a jug to her lips, said, “God bless it to you, Grethel,” and took a good pull.
sentences.n: The subject is dropped again — “[sie] lief hinab” — which gives the sentence a hurried, muttering pace. ansetzen here is to put the vessel to one’s lips; gesegnes = gesegne es, the old blessing spoken over a drink, which she pronounces over herself.

sentences.t: „Der Wein hängt an einander,“ sprachs weiter, „und ist nicht gut abbrechen,“ und that noch einen ernsthaften Zug.
sentences.l: “The wine hangs together,” it spoke further, “and it is not good to break off,” and took yet another serious draught.
sentences.i: “Wine hangs together,” she went on, “and it is not good to break it off” — and took another serious pull.
sentences.n: A drinker’s proverb: the wine is all of one piece, so it is wrong to stop in the middle. abbrechen = to break off, leave unfinished. sprachs = sprach es.

sentences.t: Nun gieng es und stellte die Hühner wieder übers Feuer, strich sie mit Butter und trieb den Spieß lustig herum.
sentences.l: Now it went and set the chickens again over the fire, brushed them with butter and drove the spit merrily around.
sentences.i: Now she went and set the chickens over the fire again, brushed them with butter and turned the spit merrily round.

sentences.t: Weil aber der Braten so gut roch, dachte Grethel „es könnte etwas fehlen, versucht muß er werden!“
sentences.l: But because the roast smelled so good, Grethel thought “something could be lacking, tasted must it be!”
sentences.i: But because the roast smelled so good, Grethel thought: “Something might be wanting — it must be tasted!”

sentences.t: schleckte mit dem Finger und sprach „ei, was sind die Hühner so gut! ist ja Sünd und Schand, daß man sie nicht gleich ißt!“
sentences.l: licked with the finger and spoke “ei, how good the chickens are! it is indeed sin and shame that one does not eat them at once!”
sentences.i: She took a lick with her finger and said: “Why, how good these chickens are! It is a sin and a shame not to eat them at once!”
sentences.n: was is the exclamatory “how” (modern wie). “Sünd und Schand” is a fixed pair, clipped in speech from Sünde und Schande.

sentences.t: Lief zum Fenster, ob der Herr mit dem Gast noch nicht käm, aber es sah niemand:
sentences.l: Ran to the window, whether the master with the guest were not yet coming, but it saw nobody:
sentences.i: She ran to the window to see whether the master and the guest were not coming yet, but she saw no one.

sentences.t: stellte sich wieder zu den Hühnern, dachte „der eine Flügel verbrennt, besser ists, ich eß ihn weg.“
sentences.l: placed itself again by the chickens, thought “the one wing is burning, better it is, I eat it away.”
sentences.i: She placed herself by the chickens again, and thought: “One wing is burning — better that I eat it up.”

sentences.t: Also schnitt es ihn ab, und aß ihn auf, und er schmeckte ihm: und wie es damit fertig war, dachte es „der andere muß auch herab, sonst merkt der Herr daß etwas fehlt.“
sentences.l: So it cut it off, and ate it up, and it tasted good to it: and when it was finished with that, it thought “the other must down too, otherwise the master notices that something is missing.”
sentences.i: So she cut it off and ate it up, and it tasted good to her; and when she had finished with it she thought: “The other must come off too, or the master will notice that something is missing.”

sentences.t: Wie die zwei Flügel verzehrt waren, gieng es wieder und schaute nach dem Herrn, und sah ihn nicht.
sentences.l: When the two wings were consumed, it went again and looked out for the master, and saw him not.
sentences.i: When the two wings had been consumed, she went again and looked out for the master, and did not see him.

sentences.t: „Wer weiß,“ fiel ihm ein, „sie kommen wohl gar nicht, und sind wo eingekehrt.“
sentences.l: “Who knows,” it occurred to it, “they are probably not coming at all, and have stopped in somewhere.”
sentences.i: “Who knows,” it struck her, “perhaps they are not coming at all, and have turned in somewhere on the way.”
sentences.n: “es fällt jemandem ein” = it occurs to someone. einkehren is to stop at an inn for a drink — she charges the two men with exactly what she is doing. wo is a clipped irgendwo, somewhere.

sentences.t: Da sprachs „hei, Grethel, sei guter Dinge, das eine ist doch angegriffen, thu noch einen frischen Trunk, und iß es vollends auf, wenns all ist, hast du Ruhe: warum soll die gute Gottesgabe umkommen?“
sentences.l: Then it spoke “hei, Grethel, be of good things, the one is broached after all, take yet a fresh drink, and eat it wholly up, when it is all gone, you have peace: why should the good gift-of-God perish?”
sentences.i: Then she said: “Come, Grethel, be of good cheer! The one is broached already; take another fresh drink and eat it clean up — once it is gone you will have peace. Why should the good gift of God go to waste?”
sentences.n: “guter Dinge sein” = to be of good cheer, an old genitive phrase. angreifen here is to broach, to start in on something; all is the old sense of used up, gone. Gottesgabe, God’s gift, means food — letting it spoil would be the real sin, and that is the argument she settles on.

sentences.t: Also lief es noch einmal in den Keller, that einen ehrbaren Trunk, und aß das eine Huhn in aller Freudigkeit auf.
sentences.l: So it ran once more into the cellar, took an honorable drink, and ate the one chicken up in all joyfulness.
sentences.i: So she ran down to the cellar once more, took an honorable drink, and ate the one chicken up in perfect gladness.
sentences.n: The adjectives on her drinks keep rising in dignity as she sinks: a guten Zug, an ernsthaften Zug, a frischen Trunk, now an ehrbaren — an honorable one — with a herzhafter still to come.

sentences.t: Wie das eine Huhn hinunter war, und der Herr noch immer nicht kam, sah Grethel das andere an, und sprach „wo das eine ist muß das andere auch sein, die zwei gehören zusammen: was dem einen Recht ist, das ist dem andern billig; ich glaube wenn ich noch einen Trunk thue, so sollte mirs nicht schaden.“
sentences.l: When the one chicken was down, and the master still did not come, Grethel looked at the other, and spoke “where the one is the other must be too, the two belong together: what is right for the one, that is fair for the other; I believe if I take another drink, it should not harm me.”
sentences.i: When the one chicken was down and the master still did not come, Grethel looked at the other and said: “Where the one is, the other must be too — the two belong together. What is right for the one is fair for the other; and I believe that if I take another drink, it will do me no harm.”
sentences.n: “was dem einen Recht ist, das ist dem andern billig” is a proverb of even-handed justice, with billig in its old sense of fair, not cheap. She is applying the law of equity to two roast chickens.

sentences.t: Also that es noch einen herzhaften Trunk, und ließ das zweite Huhn wieder zum andern laufen.
sentences.l: So it took yet another hearty drink, and let the second chicken run again to the other.
sentences.i: So she took another hearty drink, and let the second chicken run off after the first.

sentences.t: Wie es so im besten essen war, kam der Herr daher gegangen, und rief „eil dich, Grethel, der Gast kommt gleich nach.“
sentences.l: As it was thus in the best eating, came the master along, and called “hurry yourself, Grethel, the guest is coming right after.”
sentences.i: While she was in the very thick of her eating, the master came along and called: “Make haste, Grethel, the guest is coming right behind me.”
sentences.n: “im besten essen sein” = to be in the thick of eating; the infinitive essen is used as a noun and the 1857 text leaves it lowercase.

sentences.t: „Ja, Herr, wills schon zurichten,“ antwortete Grethel.
sentences.l: “Yes, sir, will already prepare it,” answered Grethel.
sentences.i: “Yes, sir, I’ll have it ready,” answered Grethel.

sentences.t: Der Herr sah indessen ob der Tisch wohl gedeckt war, nahm das große Messer, womit er die Hühner zerschneiden wollte, und wetzte es auf dem Gang.
sentences.l: The master looked meanwhile whether the table was well laid, took the great knife with which he wanted to cut up the chickens, and whetted it in the passage.
sentences.i: The master meanwhile looked whether the table was properly laid, took the great knife he meant to carve the chickens with, and whetted it out in the passage.
sentences.n: Gang is the passage or hallway of the house. Everything Grethel’s lie will need is now in place: an innocent knife, and a guest at the door.

sentences.t: Indem kam der Gast, klopfte sittig und höflich an der Hausthüre.
sentences.l: In that moment came the guest, knocked decorously and politely at the house-door.
sentences.i: Just then the guest came, and knocked at the front door, decorous and polite.

sentences.t: Grethel lief und schaute wer da war, und als es den Gast sah, hielt es den Finger an den Mund und sprach „still! still!
sentences.l: Grethel ran and looked who was there, and when it saw the guest, it held the finger to the mouth and spoke “quiet! quiet!
sentences.i: Grethel ran and looked to see who was there; and when she saw the guest she held her finger to her lips and said: “Hush! hush!

sentences.t: macht geschwind daß ihr wieder fort kommt, wenn euch mein Herr erwischt, so seid ihr unglücklich; er hat euch zwar zum Nachtessen eingeladen, aber er hat nichts anders im Sinn, als euch die beiden Ohren abzuschneiden.
sentences.l: make quickly that you get away again, if my master catches you, so you are unfortunate; he has indeed invited you to the night-meal, but he has nothing else in mind than to cut off both your ears.
sentences.i: See that you get away, and quickly — if my master catches you, you are lost. He did invite you to supper, true enough, but he has nothing else in mind than cutting off both your ears.
sentences.n: “macht daß ihr fort kommt” = see to it that you get away, a brisk idiom. Nachtessen is the evening meal. zwar… aber makes the concession and then takes it back: he did invite you, but…

sentences.t: Hört nur wie er das Messer dazu wetzt.“
sentences.l: Only hear how he whets the knife for it.”
sentences.i: Only listen how he is whetting the knife for it.”

sentences.t: Der Gast hörte das Wetzen und eilte was er konnte die Stiegen wieder hinab.
sentences.l: The guest heard the whetting and hurried what he could down the stairs again.
sentences.i: The guest heard the whetting and hurried back down the stairs as fast as he could.
sentences.n: “eilte was er konnte” = hurried as much as he could, the bare was-clause doing the work of “as fast as.” Stiegen is the southern word for stairs, still ordinary in Austria and Bavaria.

sentences.t: Grethel war nicht faul, lief schreiend zu dem Herrn und rief „da habt ihr einen schönen Gast eingeladen!“
sentences.l: Grethel was not lazy, ran screaming to the master and cried “there you have invited a fine guest!”
sentences.i: Grethel was not slow about it: she ran screaming to her master and cried, “A fine guest you have invited there!”
sentences.n: “nicht faul sein” = to lose no time, to act without hesitating. schön is pure irony. She addresses her master with the older respectful ihr (habt ihr).

sentences.t: „Ei, warum, Grethel? was meinst du damit?“
sentences.l: “Ei, why, Grethel? what do you mean by that?”
sentences.i: “Why, what for, Grethel? What do you mean by that?”

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sagte es, „der hat mir beide Hühner, die ich eben auftragen wollte, von der Schüssel genommen und ist damit fortgelaufen.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” it said, “that one has taken from me both chickens, which I just wanted to carry in, off the dish and has run away with them.”
sentences.i: “Why,” said she, “that fellow took both the chickens off the dish — the very ones I was about to carry in — and ran off with them.”
sentences.n: der is a demonstrative used dismissively of a person: that one, that fellow. auftragen is to carry a dish to the table; mir is the dative of the person wronged.

sentences.t: „Das ist feine Weise!“ sprach der Herr, und ward ihm leid um die schönen Hühner, „wenn er mir dann wenigstens das eine gelassen hätte, damit mir was zu essen geblieben wäre.“
sentences.l: “That is a fine manner!” spoke the master, and it became sorry to him about the fine chickens, “if he had then at least left me the one, so that something to eat would have remained to me.”
sentences.i: “That is a pretty way to behave!” said the master, and he grew sorry over the fine chickens. “If he had at least left me the one, so that something would have been left me to eat.”
sentences.n: “es ward ihm leid um…” is impersonal — it grew sorry to him about the chickens, that is, he regretted them. ward is the old past of werden. His whole grief is for the birds.

sentences.t: Er rief ihm nach er sollte bleiben, aber der Gast that als hörte er es nicht.
sentences.l: He called after him he should stay, but the guest did as though he heard it not.
sentences.i: He called after him to stay, but the guest acted as though he did not hear.

sentences.t: Da lief er hinter ihm her, das Messer noch immer in der Hand, und schrie „nur eins! nur eins!“
sentences.l: Then he ran after him, the knife still always in the hand, and shouted “only one! only one!”
sentences.i: Then he ran after him, the knife still in his hand, shouting: “Only one! Only one!”
sentences.n: eins is neuter, and so is both das Huhn and das Ohr: one chicken to the master, one ear to the guest. The whole tale folds into that one word.

sentences.t: und meinte, der Gast sollte ihm nur ein Huhn lassen, und nicht alle beide nehmen:
sentences.l: and meant, the guest should leave him only one chicken, and not take both of them:
sentences.i: and he meant that the guest should leave him just one chicken and not take them both;

sentences.t: der Gast aber meinte nicht anders, als er sollte eins von seinen Ohren hergeben, und lief als wenn Feuer unter ihm brennte, damit er sie beide heimbrächte.
sentences.l: the guest however meant it no otherwise than that he should hand over one of his ears, and ran as if fire were burning under him, so that he might bring them both home.
sentences.i: but the guest took it to mean nothing else than that he was to give up one of his ears, and ran as though fire were burning under him, that he might bring them both home.
sentences.n: “nicht anders meinen, als…” = to take it to mean nothing else than. brennte is the subjunctive of brennen in an unreal comparison; sie beide are his two ears. Nobody in the tale ever learns what became of the chickens.
